newsitem.title: USA: US June retail sales up, but not seen swaying Fed.
newsitem.headline: US June retail sales up, but not seen swaying Fed.

text.p: A higher-than-expected 0.5-percent increase in U.S. June retail sales data suggests the consumer is still fairly active, but the figure on its own won't be enough to influence monetary policy, analysts said.

"Some of the discretionary items were the stronger categories of the report, but still not enough yet to alarm the Federal Reserve," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.

The Commerce Department released its seasonally adjusted data on retail sales on Tuesday. The overall headline number showed purchases increased by 0.5 percent in June, above Wall Street expectations for a 0.2-percent rise.

The May overall index was revised down to a 0.3-percent fall against a previously announced 0.1-percent drop. The ex-automobile index, however, rose 0.3 percent in June, well below the 0.5-percent jump expected by forecasters.
"The numbers don't show a consumer that is coming back with any kind of a spending vengeance," said James Padinha, economist at consulting firm Briefing.com.

"But the flipside of that is that the numbers show that the April and May low (in consumer spending) was exactly that. Following a little bit of derailment, we seem to be back on track now," Padinha said.

Although not seen enough to sway the Fed, analysts said the June retail sales report was likely to pour cold water on some theories that the economy would continue to slow by itself through the rest of the year.

"A lot of the fundamentals point to reports as strong or stronger than this one. For people looking for no more moves from the Fed and even an easing in 1998 ... this (report) is clearly bad for that scenario," Briefing.com's Padinha said.
"This report certainly rules out the notion of the dead consumer," he added.
Analysts said one of the biggest surprises of the report was a large jump in auto sales. But some Wall Street experts said the 1.1 percent rise could have been somewhat overstated.
"The auto component is probably not up 1.1 (percent).

"The Commerce Department historically has a problem coordinating their survey of car sales and actual car sales, and June appears to be a month when they overstated the auto components," Sanwa's Strauss said.
In addition, Commerce said durable goods sales were up 0.5 percent, while the building materials component dropped by 1.2 percent.

"(The report) is showing the consumer is still very cautious at the end of the second quarter and doesn't change the expectation that we'll see a good bounce in the third quarter," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBS Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
The Fed last changed interest rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The central bank then stood pat at its May and July policy meetings.
